doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

title: Projection learned from elders and brass bands
summary: White cites the Afro-Creole clarinet tradition, Willie Humphrey's projection and four years in brass bands as the source of his tone and projection.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well you know I’m very much coming out of the traditional New Orleans, the Afro- Creole clarinet tradition. And I got to hear nine players that were born before 1912. And they all had these special unique sounds and tones, and you know I just learned a lot about projection. I mean Willie Humphrey, who had perhaps a generally thinner tone in the upper register, could project through anything. And he told me a lot about projection but also I started out playing in brass bands. I played four years in brass bands in community black social club parades, jazz funerals, and church parades. And in a brass band, you know you have to learn how to really project to cut through those lot of instruments. So I guess I focused on tone and projection. So that’s always an important thing for me. You always have to put – you know not overblow, but you always have to put a steady amount of air in the horn and, you know, maintain that.
